sections.title: Flat Dilatometer
sections.summary: DMT dissipation tests give ch (section 6.13), and with mv = 1/M estimated from the dilatometer modulus ED (Chapter 8), k follows from Eq. 10.28.
sections.body: Hydraulic conductivity can be estimated from DMT time-pressure dissipation tests with Eq. 10.28: ch from the DMT dissipation test (section 6.13) and mv = 1/M estimated from the dilatometer modulus ED (Chapter 8). (p. 10-55)
key_points: mv = 1/M estimated from the dilatometer modulus ED (p. 10-55).
sections.applicability: Field and laboratory hydraulic conductivity measurement and estimation from correlations

sections.title: BAT Probe
sections.summary: The BAT groundwater sampling probe (sintered porous element behind a 60-degree cone) with an auxiliary pressure transducer kit (Figure 10-38) measures gas pressure change in a sealed evacuated vial; by Boyle's law k follows from Eq. 10.31 as printed.
sections.body: The BAT system samples groundwater at discrete depths with a hermetically sealed technique: a stainless steel body with a sintered stainless steel porous element behind a 60-degree conical point, resembling a piezocone but measuring no force or pore pressure; a septum seals the probe. For k, an auxiliary kit (pressure transducer and readout, Figure 10-38, Trautwein and Boutwell, 1994, p. 10-56) lowers an evacuated sealed glass vial on extension rods; a double-ended hypodermic needle connects probe and vial and gas pressure change is recorded. By Boyle's law the pressure change gives a volume change and k (Eq. 10.31), with Po the initial gas pressure and Vo the initial gas volume in the vial, Pt the average measured pressure between t1 and t, P3 the net pressure applied to the chamber, Pt/t the rate of change of pressure and F a shape factor. (pp. 10-55 to 10-56)
key_points: Porous element behind a 60-degree conical point; no force or pore pressure measured (p. 10-55).
Boyle's law converts vial pressure change to volume change (p. 10-55).
equations: Eq. 10.31: k = (Po Vo / F)(1 / ((Pt^2 P3)(Pt/t))) (as printed); Po = initial gas pressure in the vial, Vo = initial gas volume in the vial, Pt = average measured pressure between t1 and t, P3 = net pressure applied to the chamber, Pt/t = rate of change of pressure, F = shape factor (p. 10-56)
figures: Figure 10-38: BAT system for determining hydraulic conductivity (from Trautwein and Boutwell, 1994)
sections.applicability: Field and laboratory hydraulic conductivity measurement and estimation from correlations

sections.title: Estimation of Hydraulic Conductivity from Correlations
sections.summary: For preliminary design, estimate k from more easily measured soil properties, with engineering judgment, rather than guessing: grain size and density for granular soils (section 10.15.1), void ratio for fine-grained soils (section 10.15.2).
sections.body: Approximate k estimates for preliminary design can be made by several approaches with engineering judgment; it is more desirable to base initial estimates on other more easily measured soil properties than simply to guess. (p. 10-56)
key_points: Estimate k from easily measured properties rather than guessing (p. 10-56).
sections.applicability: Field and laboratory hydraulic conductivity measurement and estimation from correlations

sections.title: Estimating Hydraulic Conductivity for Granular Soils
sections.summary: For granular soils grain size and density govern k (Figure 10-39). Hazen (1911): k = C D10^2 (Eq. 10.32), cm/s with D10 in cm, C about 90 to 120 (often 100). Shepherd (1989): k = c d^2, c = a x^b (Eqs. 10.33, 10.34). Carrier (2003): Kozeny-Carman k = 1.99 x 10^4 Deff^2 (1/SF^2)(e^3/(1 + e)) (Eqs. 10.35, 10.36) for silts, sands and gravelly sands at 20 degrees C.
sections.body: Grain size characteristics (mean size, gradation, uniformity coefficient) and density (void ratio, porosity) are the two most important factors (Figure 10-39, Sevee, 2006, p. 10-57). Hazen (1911), from clean loose sand, Eq. 10.32: k in cm/s, D10 the effective size in cm, C typically about 90 to 120, often 100 (p. 10-58). Shepherd (1989), Eq. 10.33 (c a constant for all factors other than grain size, d particle diameter); from 19 published data sets, c = a x^b (Eq. 10.34) with x = D50; a about 1000 to 200,000 for k in gallons/day/ft2, b about 1.1 to 2.0. Carrier (2003) recommends Kozeny-Carman, accounting for grain size and density (Eq. 10.35): k in cm/s, Deff the effective grain size in cm (Eq. 10.36, fi the fraction between two sieves, Dl-i and Ds-i the larger and smaller openings, summed over all sieves), e void ratio, SF a shape factor of 6.6 rounded, 7.5 medium angularity, 8.4 angular (Loudon, 1952). Not appropriate for clayey soils or gravelly soils with non-laminar flow; appropriate for silts, sands and gravelly sands; strictly for 20 degrees C, with other forms for other temperatures (Carrier, 2003) (p. 10-59). (pp. 10-57 to 10-59)
key_points: Grain size and density are the two most important factors (p. 10-57).
Hazen C typically 90 to 120, often 100 (p. 10-58).
Shepherd a about 1000 to 200,000 (gallons/day/ft2), b about 1.1 to 2.0 (p. 10-58).
SF = 6.6 rounded, 7.5 medium angularity, 8.4 angular (Loudon, 1952) (p. 10-58).
Kozeny-Carman not for clayey or gravelly soils with non-laminar flow (p. 10-59).
equations: Eq. 10.32: k = C x D10^2 (Hazen, 1911); k in cm/s, C = constant (typically 90 to 120, often 100), D10 = effective grain size (10 percent finer) in cm (p. 10-57)
Eq. 10.33: k = c d^2 (Shepherd, 1989); c = constant, d = particle diameter (p. 10-58)
Eq. 10.34: c = a x^b; x = mean grain size D50, a and b = regression coefficients (p. 10-58)
Eq. 10.35: k = 1.99 x 10^4 x Deff^2 x (1/SF^2) x (e^3/(1 + e)) (Kozeny-Carman; Carrier, 2003); k in cm/s, Deff = effective grain size in cm, SF = shape factor, e = void ratio; 20 degrees C (p. 10-58)
Eq. 10.36: Deff = 100% / sum(fi / (Dl-i^0.404 x Ds-i^0.595)); fi = fraction of particles between two sieve sizes, Dl-i, Ds-i = larger and smaller sieve openings (p. 10-58)

sections.title: Estimating Hydraulic Conductivity for Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: In fine-grained soils void ratio governs k: log k vs. e is nearly linear for a clay (Figure 10-40) but differs between clays by over 2 orders of magnitude (Figure 10-41), converging at e about 0.2 to 0.3. Mesri et al. (1994): k = 6.5 x 10^-11 [(e/CF)/(Ac + 1)]^4 m/s (Eq. 10.37); Tavenas et al. (1983): Ck = 0.5(e) (Eq. 10.38), Ck about 0.4 to 1.6.
sections.body: Porosity or void ratio is the most important factor because particle sizes span a small range, mostly below 0.074 mm (No. 200 sieve), so packing matters; pore-size distribution controls k but is hard to quantify routinely. For a given clay k and void ratio are fairly uniquely related, log k vs. e nearly linear (Figure 10-40, Leroueil et al., 1990, p. 10-60); different soft clays differ by more than 2 orders of magnitude at a fixed void ratio (Figure 10-41, Terzaghi et al., 1996), converging near e of 0.2 to 0.3. Mesri et al. (1994), accounting for clay content and mineralogy: Eq. 10.37 with k in m/s, CF the clay size fraction (percent < 0.002 mm) and Ac = PI/CF the activity. The change of permeability index Ck = delta e/delta log k; Tavenas et al. (1983) relate it to in situ void ratio for soft clays by Eq. 10.38; large Ck means small changes in k; typical soft clay Ck about 0.4 to 1.6. (pp. 10-59 to 10-60)
key_points: Void ratio is the most important factor for fine-grained soils (p. 10-59).
Soft clays differ by more than 2 orders of magnitude in k at a fixed e (p. 10-59).
Ck = delta e/delta log k (p. 10-59).
Typical soft clay Ck about 0.4 to 1.6 (p. 10-60).
equations: Eq. 10.37: k = 6.5 x 10^-11 [(e/CF)/(Ac + 1)]^4 (Mesri et al., 1994); k in m/s, e = void ratio, CF = clay size fraction (percent < 0.002 mm), Ac = PI/CF = clay activity (p. 10-59)
Eq. 10.38: Ck = 0.5(e) (Tavenas et al., 1983); Ck = delta e/delta log k, e = in situ void ratio (p. 10-59)
